answerNotes.LABEL: A label identifies an item or its contents. It can carry a name, date, size, or address depending on the scene.
answerNotes.SEED: A seed contains the beginning of a new plant. A seed packet's planting instructions describe how to help it start growing.
answerNotes.DATE: A date identifies a day, usually with a month and year. It can distinguish a photo's occasion from the day its note was written.
answerNotes.NAME: A name identifies a person or thing. In a family album, adding names helps later readers recognize the people pictured.
answerNotes.ROW: A row is a line of things side by side. Garden plants, theater seats, and letters in a puzzle can all be arranged in rows.
answerNotes.PENCIL: The writing core of a modern pencil is graphite, not metallic lead. Lead remains a traditional everyday name for it.
answerNotes.SOIL: Soil is the material around garden roots. It contains more than loose mineral particles: air, water, and decaying material are also part of it.
answerNotes.LIGHT: Light makes things visible. A lamp produces light, while a mirror mainly reflects light arriving from elsewhere.
answerNotes.ROOT: Roots anchor a plant and take up water from the soil. They are below the stem, even when part of a root is visible above ground.

answerNotes.JAR: A jar has a wide opening that makes spooning and filling easier. A bottle usually has a narrower neck.
answerNotes.PAPER: Paper can be folded, cut, and written on. Card stock is heavier and stiffer, making it useful for tags and greeting cards.
answerNotes.ROOT: Roots anchor a plant and take up water from the soil. They are below the stem, even when part of a root is visible above ground.
answerNotes.GLASS: Glass is usually transparent but can also be colored. A glass is a drinking vessel, while glass without an article can name the material.
answerNotes.WHITE: White is a color description, not a flower or bird name. Crossings can help when a clue asks for a color rather than a species.
answerNotes.GREEN: Green describes many growing leaves. It is also a color name in its own right, so read whether the clue asks for a plant or its appearance.
answerNotes.SEED: A seed contains the beginning of a new plant. A seed packet's planting instructions describe how to help it start growing.
answerNotes.WATCH: Watch can be a wrist timepiece or the action of looking attentively. A football-viewing scene uses the action rather than the object.
answerNotes.LEAF: Leaves use light to help a plant make food. The flat blade and its veins are useful details to notice when identifying a leaf.

answerNotes.ROW: A row is a line of things side by side. Garden plants, theater seats, and letters in a puzzle can all be arranged in rows.
answerNotes.BULB: A bulb stores food for a plant underground. Tulips and daffodils grow from bulbs rather than from a packet of seed each spring.
answerNotes.WHITE: White is a color description, not a flower or bird name. Crossings can help when a clue asks for a color rather than a species.
answerNotes.ROOT: Roots anchor a plant and take up water from the soil. They are below the stem, even when part of a root is visible above ground.
answerNotes.SOIL: Soil is the material around garden roots. It contains more than loose mineral particles: air, water, and decaying material are also part of it.
answerNotes.STRING: String is a thin cord used for tying or flying a kite. A kite's string connects the flying frame to the person holding it.
answerNotes.LINE: Line can mean a row, a drawn mark, or a fishing cord. The clue's action helps distinguish those meanings.

answerNotes.PICK: Pick can mean choose or pluck. In a harvest setting, it usually means gathering something from the plant.
answerNotes.GREEN: Green describes many growing leaves. It is also a color name in its own right, so read whether the clue asks for a plant or its appearance.
answerNotes.KNIFE: A knife cuts with a blade. In the kitchen, the board beneath the food supports the ingredient while it is sliced.
answerNotes.STEM: A stem supports leaves and flowers. It also connects the plant's growing parts with the roots below.
answerNotes.FLOWER: A flower is the blossom, rather than the whole plant. In everyday speech, the word can also describe a plant grown for its blooms.
answerNotes.SLICE: A slice is a flat cut portion of food. Slice can also be the action of cutting food into those portions.
answerNotes.BAKE: Baking uses dry heat in an oven. Boiling instead cooks food in bubbling liquid.
answerNotes.BASKET: A basket is made by weaving flexible material. Its open structure and carrying handle make it useful for collecting garden produce.
answerNotes.LEAF: Leaves use light to help a plant make food. The flat blade and its veins are useful details to notice when identifying a leaf.
answerNotes.SUMMER: Summer scenes use familiar warm-weather outings. Actual temperatures and traditions differ between regions and families.
